narrative:
The 2026 Minnesota Twins opened the season with a familiar blend of promise and frustration. April saw the offense flash real potential — Austin Martin's clutch double and Ryan Jeffers' grand slam generated genuine excitement — but the pitching staff, particularly the bullpen, was already showing cracks. Blown leads and costly extra-base hits surrendered defined these early weeks, setting a shaky foundation for a team that could never quite stabilize.

May and June brought more of the same turbulence. Taylor Rogers' disastrous blown save against Pittsburgh on May 29th — surrendering a two-run homer to Bryan Reynolds in what became the season's single most damaging play — crystallized the bullpen's unreliability. Joe Ryan struggled to protect leads, Anthony Banda was victimized for a Hunter Goodman walk-off blast, and the relievers' collective ERA ballooned. Eric Orze became a symbol of the back-end problems, appearing in three separate high-leverage disasters across April and June. The offense, meanwhile, showed bright spots — Kody Clemens' 10th homer and Alex Jackson's clutch single — but the run prevention issues always seemed to outpace the scoring.

July sparked a rare moment of genuine belief. Royce Lewis, returning to health, delivered a stunning walk-off triple on July 28th that lit up Target Field, and Kody Clemens followed two days later with the season's most impactful single play — a go-ahead grand slam that briefly had Minnesota dreaming of a wild-card chase. The team played some of its best baseball of the year during this stretch, and the lineup's depth — with Clemens, Lewis, Brooks Lee, and the young Walker Jenkins — hinted at what this roster could become.

September, however, told the true story. The Twins entered the final month needing to nearly run the table, and instead stumbled repeatedly. A.J. Minter was tagged twice in crucial late-game spots, Yoendrys Gómez surrendered key runs against the Yankees and Angels in back-to-back series, and Mike Trout reminded everyone he still had plenty left. Walker Jenkins' homer and some late defensive gems — including a season-saving double play executed by Travis Adams — offered flickers of optimism, but they were too little, too late. Minnesota finished 77-85, eight games under .500, their playoff drought extending another year as a roster built around upside once again fell short of its potential.

chapters.title: Early Chaos: Highs and Cracks
chapters.description: April delivers both exhilarating offensive moments and alarming signs of bullpen vulnerability.

chapters.title: The Bullpen Burns
chapters.description: May's blown saves and June's mounting losses reveal a pitching staff unable to protect leads.

chapters.title: Clemens and Company Answer Back
chapters.description: The offense flares in mid-June with clutch home runs and timely hits that briefly keep the season afloat.

chapters.title: Lewis Returns, Dreams Reignite
chapters.description: Royce Lewis' electrifying triple and Kody Clemens' grand slam in late July spark a winning surge that revives playoff hopes.

chapters.title: September Fades
chapters.description: A brutal final month of bullpen collapses and timely opponent heroics extinguishes any remaining postseason hope.
